heroIntro: With hundreds of thousands of Bangladeshi citizens residing in the United States, United Kingdom, Canada, and Australia, transnational matrimonial breakdowns represent one of the most volatile areas of private international law in Bangladesh. A frequent scenario involves couples married under Bangladeshi Islamic or secular rites in Dhaka who subsequently divorce in a foreign court (e.g., obtaining a State Circuit Court dissolution in New York, a Decree Absolute in London, or an Ontario Superior Court judgment). When one party returns to Bangladesh to remarry, claim ancestral dower/denmohor, or custody of minor children, they often face a severe legal shock: **a foreign divorce decree is not automatically valid or self-executing in Bangladesh**. Under **Section 13 of the Code of Civil Procedure 1908 (CPC)** and the **Muslim Family Laws Ordinance 1961 (MFLO)**, foreign judgments must meet stringent statutory tests. Failing to serve statutory notices under Section 7 MFLO can result in charges of bigamy (Section 494 Penal Code) or denial of marital rights. This guide provides an authoritative legal breakdown of how to validate or challenge a foreign divorce in Bangladesh.

quickAnswer.title: Quick Overview: Is a Foreign Divorce Decree Valid in Bangladesh?
quickAnswer.text: A foreign divorce decree is recognized in Bangladesh only if it satisfies the criteria laid down in Section 13 of the Code of Civil Procedure 1908 (CPC) AND complies with mandatory domestic family laws. Under Section 13 CPC, a foreign judgment is conclusive as to any matter directly adjudicated upon, EXCEPT where: (a) it was pronounced by a court lacking competent international jurisdiction; (b) it was not given on the merits; (c) it was founded on an incorrect view of international law or refusal to recognize Bangladeshi personal law; (d) proceedings were opposed to natural justice (e.g. ex-parte without proper summons); (e) it was obtained by fraud; or (f) it sustains a claim founded on a breach of Bangladeshi law. Furthermore, for Muslim couples, Section 7 of the Muslim Family Laws Ordinance 1961 mandates that written notice must still be served on the local Union Parishad or City Corporation Mayor with a 90-day reconciliation window. Merely possessing a foreign court paper without domestic compliance leaves the marriage legally alive in Bangladesh.
highlights: Governing Law: Code of Civil Procedure 1908 (Sections 13 & 14), Muslim Family Laws Ordinance 1961 (Section 7), Family Courts Act 2023, Penal Code 1860 (Section 494).
Section 13 CPC Rule: Foreign judgments are conclusive unless they violate one of the six statutory exceptions (lack of jurisdiction, non-merit, natural justice violation, fraud, etc.).

Ex-Parte Foreign Decrees: If one spouse remained in Bangladesh and was never legally served or given a reasonable opportunity to appear, the foreign divorce is void ab initio for violating natural justice.

Mandatory Section 7 MFLO Notice: The foreign decree must be submitted alongside a formal Talaq Notice to the relevant City Corporation Mayor / UP Chairman in Bangladesh, followed by the mandatory 90-day cooling-off period.

Risk of Bigamy: Remarrying in Bangladesh relying solely on an unvalidated foreign decree exposes the individual to criminal prosecution under Section 494 of the Penal Code (imprisonment up to 7 years).
Dower (Denmohar) & Maintenance: Foreign divorce judgments that terminate marital dower or child maintenance contrary to Bangladeshi Muslim personal law are non-binding on Bangladeshi Family Courts.
Judicial Declaratory Suit: The safest course is filing a Declaratory Suit under Section 42 of the Specific Relief Act 1877 in a Bangladeshi Family Court to obtain formal recognition.

sections.title: 1. Section 13 CPC: The Six Grounds for Refusing Foreign Divorce Decrees
sections.content:
Unlike treaties in the European Union, Bangladesh does not have automatic reciprocal divorce recognition treaties with Western countries. Recognition of foreign judgments is strictly governed by Section 13 of the Code of Civil Procedure 1908 (CPC), which establishes that a foreign judgment is conclusive between the parties, except under six statutory circumstances:

  1. Section 13(a) - Lack of Competent Jurisdiction: Where the foreign court had no international jurisdiction over the parties (e.g., neither party had true domicile or habitual residence in that foreign country).
  2. Section 13(b) - Not Given on the Merits: Where the decree was passed mechanically without judicial examination of evidence or pleadings.
  3. Section 13(c) - Refusal to Recognize Bangladeshi Law: Where the judgment founded on an incorrect view of international law or refused to recognize the substantive personal law of Bangladesh applicable to the parties.
  4. Section 13(d) - Opposed to Natural Justice: Where the proceedings were conducted without proper citation, service of summons, or notice to the responding spouse.
  5. Section 13(e) - Obtained by Fraud: Where the petitioner lied about their residence, forged service certificates, or concealed material facts from the foreign judge.
  6. Section 13(f) - Sustaining Breach of Bangladeshi Law: Where the decree enforces an outcome that violates fundamental domestic public policy (e.g., depriving a Muslim wife of her vested dower rights).

sections.title: 2. The Section 7 MFLO Requirement: Talaq Notice & 90-Day Arbitration
sections.content:
Even where a foreign decree satisfies Section 13 CPC, Muslim citizens of Bangladesh remain bound by the mandatory statutory framework of Section 7 of the Muslim Family Laws Ordinance 1961 (MFLO).

The Appellate Division of the Supreme Court of Bangladesh has repeatedly affirmed that dissolution of a Muslim marriage requires serving formal written notice upon the Chairman of the Union Parishad or Mayor of the City Corporation, with a copy dispatched to the wife. The marriage is not legally dissolved until the expiration of ninety (90) days from the receipt of such notice, during which the Arbitration Council must attempt reconciliation. If a foreign decree is never served upon the relevant local administrative authority in Bangladesh, the divorce remains incomplete under Bangladeshi law.

sections.title: 3. The Danger of Ex-Parte Foreign Decrees & Natural Justice Violations
sections.content:
A notorious tactic employed by spouses living abroad is filing for divorce in a US county or Australian court while the other spouse is temporarily residing in Bangladesh, deliberately providing an incorrect foreign address to procure an Ex-Parte Default Judgment.

Under Bangladeshi law, an ex-parte foreign divorce procured without actual personal service upon the resident spouse is a nullity. Under Section 13(d) of the CPC, proceedings conducted in violation of natural justice (audi alteram partem—hear the other side) have zero legal force in Bangladesh. The resident spouse can ignore the foreign judgment and institute independent proceedings in a Bangladeshi Family Court for restitution of conjugal rights, recovery of dower, or maintenance.

sections.title: 4. Impact on Dower (Denmohar), Maintenance & Child Custody
sections.content:
Foreign divorce judgments in the West frequently attempt to adjudicate global asset splits, wiping out spousal support or omitting the Islamic requirement of Dower (Denmohar). In Bangladeshi jurisprudence:

  • Dower is Non-Negotiable: Under Section 10 of the Family Courts Act 2023 and Muslim personal law, dower is an absolute statutory debt payable to the wife upon dissolution. A foreign court decree that purports to extinguish dower without the wife's express Islamic relinquishment violates Section 13(f) CPC and will be disregarded by Bangladeshi Family Courts.
  • Child Custody (Hizanat): Western custody orders granting sole custody to one parent based on 'best interests' do not automatically override the Guardians and Wards Act 1890 in Bangladesh. The Bangladeshi Family Court retains plenary welfare jurisdiction over minor children physically present inside Bangladesh.

sections.title: 5. Remarriage Pitfalls: Section 494 Penal Code Bigamy Prosecutions
sections.content:
The gravest danger of an unvalidated foreign divorce is entering into a second marriage in Bangladesh. If a husband or wife obtains a foreign divorce decree in Toronto or London, flies to Dhaka, and marries another person without completing Section 7 MFLO notices or obtaining a Section 42 Declaratory Decree:

  • The original marriage remains subsisting in the eyes of Bangladeshi law.
  • The abandoned spouse can file a criminal complaint under Section 494 of the Penal Code 1860 (Bigamy), which carries a punishment of rigorous imprisonment for up to seven (7) years alongside a judicial fine.
  • The second marriage is legally void, illegitimizing the status of subsequent children for inheritance purposes under Bangladeshi law.

sections.title: 7. Step-by-Step Procedure to Validate a Foreign Divorce in Bangladesh
sections.content:
To achieve ironclad legal certainty and avoid criminal or property litigation, expatriates should follow this precise legal sequence:

  1. Apostille / Consular Attestation: Obtain a certified copy of the foreign divorce judgment, authenticated by the foreign department of state / foreign office, and attested by the Embassy/High Commission of Bangladesh abroad.
  2. MOFA Counter-Attestation in Dhaka: Submit the attested decree to the Consular Wing of the Ministry of Foreign Affairs (MOFA) in Dhaka for local verification.
  3. Filing Section 7 MFLO Notice: Serve a written notice enclosing the authenticated decree upon the Mayor of the City Corporation or UP Chairman of the area where the marriage was registered, sending a copy via registered post to the other spouse.
  4. Obtaining the 90-Day Dissolution Certificate: Allow the statutory 90-day reconciliation period to lapse and secure the formal Certificate of Dissolution from the Arbitration Council.
  5. Declaratory Suit in Family Court (Recommended): File a declaratory suit under Section 42 of the Specific Relief Act 1877 before the competent Family Court, obtaining a formal decree that the foreign divorce is legally binding in Bangladesh.

sections.title: 8. How an Aggrieved Spouse Can Challenge a Fraudulent Foreign Divorce
sections.content:
If you are a spouse residing in Bangladesh and discover that your partner obtained a secret, fraudulent foreign divorce abroad:

  • File a Declaratory Suit under Section 42: Institute a suit in the Family Court praying for a judicial declaration that the foreign divorce decree is fraudulent, null, void, and inoperative under Section 13(d) and 13(e) of the CPC.
  • Claim Past & Future Maintenance: Concurrently file claims for full pending maintenance (Khorposh) and the entire unpaid prompt and deferred Dower (Denmohar) under the Family Courts Act 2023.
  • Restraining Orders: Apply for a temporary injunction restraining the defaulting spouse from remarrying in Bangladesh or taking children outside the territorial jurisdiction of Bangladesh.

sections.title: 9. Strategic Advice for NRBs in USA, UK, Canada & Australia
sections.content:
Expatriates planning a divorce must implement a dual-jurisdiction strategy right from the inception:

  • Never rely solely on a Western lawyer who lacks knowledge of Bangladeshi Muslim personal law.
  • Execute formal Talaq / Divorce notices in Bangladesh concurrently with the filing of foreign court papers to ensure the 90-day MFLO countdown runs in parallel.
  • Ensure that the dower amount stipulated in the original Bangladeshi Nikahnama (Kabinnama) is fully liquidated through verifiable banking channels, obtaining a written receipt or release deed.
  • If child custody is disputed, consult a Supreme Court advocate in Dhaka before removing minors from Bangladesh to avoid international parental kidnapping allegations under the Penal Code.

sections.title: 10. Real-Life Case Study: Overturning a Fraudulent Texas Divorce in Dhaka Family Court
sections.content:
A Bangladeshi woman residing in Dhanmondi, Dhaka, was married to a petroleum engineer based in Houston, Texas. After three years of marriage, the husband filed for divorce in a Harris County District Court in Texas, falsely claiming that his wife had abandoned him and that her whereabouts were unknown. The Texas court granted an ex-parte divorce decree by publication.

Six months later, the husband arrived in Dhaka to marry the daughter of a wealthy industrialist. The first wife retained our legal chamber. Our cross-border legal intervention unfolded as follows:

  1. Secured certified copies of the Texas decree and demonstrated that the husband was actively communicating with his wife via WhatsApp in Dhaka during the very months he swore under oath in Texas that her address was unknown.
  2. Instituted a Family Suit before the Family Court, Dhaka, challenging the foreign decree under Section 13(d) (denial of natural justice) and Section 13(e) (perjury and fraud).
  3. Concurrently filed a claim for 25 Lakh BDT unpaid Denmohar and 2 years of past maintenance.
  4. Obtained an emergency Ad-Interim Injunction from the Family Court restraining the husband from contracting a second marriage pending suit.
  5. When the husband attempted to marry regardless, our advocates filed a criminal complaint under Section 494/109 Penal Code. Faced with imminent arrest at Hazrat Shahjalal International Airport and cancellation of his US work sponsorship, the husband settled, paying the entire 25 Lakh BDT dower in full and executing a mutually agreed Islamic divorce deed.

faqs.question: Is a foreign divorce automatically valid in Bangladesh?
faqs.answer: No. A foreign divorce decree is not automatically valid. It must satisfy the legal tests of Section 13 of the Code of Civil Procedure 1908 (CPC) and, for Muslim marriages, must comply with the 90-day notice requirement under Section 7 of the Muslim Family Laws Ordinance 1961.

faqs.question: Can an ex-parte foreign divorce decree be challenged in Bangladesh?
faqs.answer: Yes. An ex-parte decree obtained without proper service of summons or notice on the spouse violates the principles of natural justice and is declared null, void, and inoperative under Section 13(d) of the CPC by Bangladeshi Family Courts.

faqs.question: Does a foreign divorce extinguish the wife's right to Dower (Denmohar)?
faqs.answer: No. Under Bangladeshi law, dower is an absolute debt under Islamic personal law. A foreign court order that purports to eliminate or waive dower without the wife's explicit consent is contrary to public policy and unenforceable in Bangladesh.

faqs.question: What happens if someone remarries in Bangladesh based solely on a foreign divorce?
faqs.answer: If the foreign divorce was not properly recognized and Section 7 MFLO notices were not served, the first marriage is still considered legally alive. Remarrying exposes the individual to criminal prosecution for bigamy under Section 494 Penal Code, carrying up to 7 years imprisonment.

faqs.question: How do you legalise a foreign divorce decree in Bangladesh?
faqs.answer: The foreign decree must be authenticated by the issuing country's authorities, attested by the Bangladesh Embassy abroad, counter-attested by MOFA in Dhaka, and submitted to the local City Corporation or Family Court alongside Section 7 MFLO procedures.

faqs.question: Can child custody decided by a US or UK court be reopened in Bangladesh?
faqs.answer: Yes. Under the Guardians and Wards Act 1890, Bangladeshi Family Courts have independent jurisdiction to decide the custody and welfare of any minor child residing within Bangladesh, regardless of foreign custody orders.

faqs.question: What is the role of Section 7 of the Muslim Family Laws Ordinance 1961?
faqs.answer: Section 7 mandates that any divorce must be formally notified in writing to the Chairman of the Union Parishad or City Corporation Mayor, followed by a mandatory 90-day reconciliation period before the divorce becomes legally effective.

faqs.question: Can an NRB contest a foreign divorce case in Dhaka without physically traveling to Bangladesh?
faqs.answer: Yes. An overseas spouse can execute a Special Power of Attorney attested by the Bangladesh Embassy abroad, empowering a Supreme Court or Family Court advocate in Dhaka to file suits, obtain injunctions, and represent them in court.
